covering.note: Wild ones are dark, mottled brownish green.

diet.note: It eats snails, fish, insects, worms and tiny water animals.

lifespan.note: In labs it can live 10 to 15 years.

clues.text: Even as an adult it keeps feathery gills sticking out behind its head.
A fin runs from the back of its head along its tail, like a tadpole's.
Wild ones are dark or black with white flecks, but labs have bred many other colors.
It grows up and breeds without ever changing into a land form, like a tadpole that never becomes a frog.
Its eggs are fertilized inside the female, and she lays them one at a time.
It lives its whole life under water.
It can regrow lost legs, gills, and even parts of its eyes and brain.
It can sense the tiny electric fields of prey.
It waits for prey to come close instead of chasing it, and its tiny teeth can grip food but not chew it.
It lives only in the canals and lakes of Xochimilco and Chalco, inside Mexico City.
Tilapia, fish that people put in its lakes, hunt it and compete for its food.

facts.text: Its name comes from the Aztec language. It may mean 'water dog', 'water twin' or 'water sprite'.
An axolotl is on Mexico's 50-peso banknote.
Its genome, the full set of its DNA, is about 10 times bigger than ours. It was the biggest animal genome ever read when it was published in 2018.
Huge numbers live in labs and homes around the world, but only 50 to 1,000 adults are left in the wild.
Lab axolotls all trace back to 34 brought from Mexico City to Paris in 1864.
Its eggs hatch after 10 to 14 days, and the young look after themselves right away.
Very rarely, when stressed, one changes into a land form, but then it can no longer breed.
Counts found about 6,000 per square kilometre in 1998, only 100 in 2008, and later just 35.
Its lakes have shrunk to under 3% of their old size, and are now marshes rather than deep lakes.
Its courtship is called a 'waltz': the pair nudge each other and circle, then the female follows the male.
